trip.start_end: Las Vegas, NV (Harry Reid International — LAS)

short.title: Low Desert Loop — the short way
short.subtitle: Death Valley · Route 66 · Palm Springs · Anza-Borrego · Joshua Tree · Needles
short.summary: The same warm loop as the long version, run in ten days instead of fourteen. Death Valley, Route 66 across the Mojave, the Coachella Valley, Anza-Borrego, Joshua Tree, and home along the old road through Needles and Kingman. Nothing sleeps above 2,200 feet and no night is expected to freeze. Be clear about the trade though: the driving is almost the same, so this is a busier trip rather than a smaller one — only two of the ten days have no driving between towns.

itinerary.headline: Below sea level by lunchtime
itinerary.notes: Pick up the vehicle and drive straight in. Furnace Creek sits 190 feet below sea level and is the warmest place you will sleep all trip — January highs around 18°C, lows around 4°C.

itinerary.headline: The whole valley floor in one day
itinerary.notes: The long version spreads this over two days. Here it is one, and it works if you start at Badwater early and finish at the dunes for sunset. What you give up is Dante's View and Mosaic Canyon, both of which need the second day.

itinerary.headline: Out of the valley and onto Route 66
itinerary.notes: The one leg that looks dull on the map, and is not. You leave Death Valley by the southern road, cross the Mojave and land on the original alignment of Route 66. Calico is a silver town that went bust in 1896 and was rebuilt as a park — kitsch, and the kids will love it.

itinerary.headline: Into the warmest air on the trip
itinerary.notes: Start on the old road for Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch, then over the pass into the Coachella Valley, which runs to 21 or 22°C in January. One night here, so take the tramway this afternoon — sunset from the top is the version worth having.

itinerary.headline: A palm oasis, then the biggest state park in California
itinerary.notes: Indian Canyons first thing, then south along the west shore of the Salton Sea — a lake 230 feet below sea level that exists only because an irrigation canal broke in 1905. You reach Borrego Springs with the afternoon still ahead of you, which is exactly enough for the sculptures and The Slot.

itinerary.headline: Out of Anza-Borrego and up to Joshua Tree
itinerary.notes: Borrego Palm Canyon before you leave — three miles round trip to a palm grove and, in a wet year, a waterfall. Then you climb about 1,500 feet and come in by Joshua Tree's south entrance, where the Cholla Cactus Garden is the first thing you meet.

itinerary.headline: A full day in Joshua Tree
itinerary.notes: Two deserts meet inside this park — the low Colorado and the high Mojave — and the Joshua trees only grow on the high side. Nearly everything worth doing is a short walk from a car park, which is what you want on the only rest day in the second half.

itinerary.headline: The empty Route 66
itinerary.notes: North on Amboy Road onto the loneliest surviving stretch of Route 66. Amboy Crater is a 250-foot cinder cone you can walk into; Roy's Motel is one neon sign in an empty town and it is the photograph everybody takes. Needles is 495 feet above sea level — the warmest bed on the whole route.

itinerary.headline: Kingman, the burros and the dam
itinerary.notes: East into Arizona for Kingman, where Route 66 crosses US-93 and the Powerhouse museum sits in a 1907 power station. Then north to Hoover Dam and into Las Vegas. In a car you can take the Oatman Highway over Sitgreaves Pass instead — ten miles shorter and half an hour slower, because it is a mountain pass with hairpins, and the wild burros come to the window.

itinerary.headline: Return and depart
itinerary.notes: Allow half a day for the vehicle return process.

rejected_extra.reason: The best red rock within an hour of Las Vegas, and the long version finishes there. It is most of what the extra four days buy you.

rejected_extra.place: A second day in Death Valley
rejected_extra.reason: One day covers Badwater, Golden Canyon, Artist's Drive and the dunes. It does not stretch to Dante's View or Mosaic Canyon — those need the day the long version has.
One night means an afternoon and a morning: The Slot and the sculptures on the way in, Borrego Palm Canyon on the way out. Font's Point and the rest of the park do not fit.

long.title: Low Desert Loop — the long way
long.subtitle: Death Valley · Palm Springs · Anza-Borrego · Joshua Tree · Route 66 · Valley of Fire
long.summary: A warm loop out of Las Vegas that never climbs into the cold. Death Valley first, then Route 66 across the Mojave, the Coachella Valley, Anza-Borrego, Joshua Tree, the old road east through Needles and Kingman, and a finish on the red rock at Valley of Fire rather than in an airport car park. Nothing sleeps above 2,600 feet, no night is expected to freeze, and five of the fourteen days involve no driving between towns.

itinerary.headline: Below sea level by lunchtime
itinerary.notes: Pick up the vehicle and drive straight in. Furnace Creek sits 190 feet below sea level and is the warmest place you will sleep all trip — January highs around 18°C, lows around 4°C.

itinerary.headline: The valley floor
itinerary.notes: Badwater Basin is the lowest point in North America. Artist's Drive is a one-way loop through mineral-stained hills and is limited to vehicles under 25 feet.

itinerary.headline: Dunes at sunrise
itinerary.notes: Mesquite Flat is twenty minutes up the valley and is best before the wind picks up. Dante's View is the one genuinely cold thing on this whole route — 5,450 feet, and it can be 14°C colder than where you parked this morning.

itinerary.headline: Out of the valley and onto Route 66
itinerary.notes: The one leg that looks dull on the map, and is not. You leave Death Valley by the southern road, cross the Mojave and land on the original alignment of Route 66. Calico is a silver town that went bust in 1896 and was rebuilt as a park — kitsch, and the kids will love it.

itinerary.headline: Into the warmest air on the trip
itinerary.notes: Start on the old road for Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch — a forest of welded steel trees hung with thousands of glass bottles, free, and unlike anything else on either version. Then over the pass into the Coachella Valley, which runs to 21 or 22°C in January. One night here, so the tramway is this afternoon.

itinerary.headline: A palm oasis, then down the Salton Sea
itinerary.notes: Indian Canyons first thing — Agua Caliente land, a real palm oasis in a desert canyon, and a walk that suits everyone. Then south along the west shore of the Salton Sea, a lake 230 feet below sea level that exists only because an irrigation canal broke in 1905 and took two years to close.

itinerary.headline: Six hundred thousand acres of state park
itinerary.notes: Borrego Palm Canyon is a three-mile round trip to a palm grove and, in a wet year, a waterfall. The Slot is a genuine slot canyon you walk yourself — no permit, no guide, no fee. Font's Point looks out over the Borrego Badlands and is the best view in the park, but the road to it is four miles of soft sand.

itinerary.headline: Up out of the low desert to Joshua Tree
itinerary.notes: You climb about 1,500 feet, and this is the first night that feels properly cool — 3 or 4°C rather than the 8 or 9°C you have had. Come in by the south entrance and the Cholla Cactus Garden is the first thing you meet.

itinerary.headline: A full day in Joshua Tree
itinerary.notes: Two deserts meet inside this park — the low Colorado and the high Mojave — and the Joshua trees only grow on the high side. Nearly everything worth doing is a short walk from a car park, which is exactly what you want on day nine with six people.

itinerary.headline: Amboy Crater and the empty Route 66
itinerary.notes: North on Amboy Road onto the loneliest surviving stretch of Route 66. Amboy Crater is a 250-foot cinder cone you can walk into. Roy's Motel is one neon sign in an empty town and it is the photograph everybody takes. Needles sits at 495 feet on the Colorado — the warmest bed on the route.

itinerary.headline: Kingman, the burros and the dam
itinerary.notes: East into Arizona for Kingman, where Route 66 crosses US-93 and the Powerhouse museum sits inside a 1907 power station. Then north to Hoover Dam and Boulder City, built in 1931 to house the men who constructed it and still the only town in Nevada where gambling is illegal. In a car you can take the Oatman Highway instead — ten miles shorter and half an hour slower, because it is a mountain pass with hairpins.

itinerary.to: Valley of Fire State Park, NV
itinerary.headline: Back to the red rock
itinerary.notes: A short morning drive that puts you inside Nevada's oldest state park with the whole afternoon left. Bright red Aztec sandstone, petroglyphs up a steel staircase at Atlatl Rock, and short walks that suit kids. All campsites are reservation-only, and there is no hotel inside the park.

itinerary.headline: The last full day, and the best rock on the route
itinerary.notes: The Fire Wave is striped red and white sandstone at the end of a short flat walk. White Domes adds a slot canyon and the remains of a 1960s film set. Elephant Rock is ten minutes from the east entrance. A better last day than a car park near the airport.

itinerary.headline: An hour and a half to the plane
itinerary.notes: Sixty-three miles to the airport, so there is time for one more walk before you go. Allow half a day for the vehicle return process.

rejected_extra.reason: A 110-mile round trip from Furnace Creek for a single crater. It fits when Death Valley gets four nights, not three.

practical_notes.warm_weather: No night on this route is expected to freeze. The coolest stops are Barstow, Twentynine Palms and Boulder City, all around 2,000 to 2,500 feet, where January lows average 3 or 4°C. A cold snap can put any of them a degree below for a few hours before dawn, so pack for 2°C nights — but there is no sustained freeze anywhere, and nothing here needs winterising.
practical_notes.booking_order: Book Palm Springs first, then Borrego Springs, then Valley of Fire if you are camping. January is high season in the Coachella Valley — the exact opposite of the Southwest Loop, where the cold made everything cheap. Death Valley, Barstow and Needles have far more slack.
practical_notes.needles: Needles is a small, faded railroad town and the lodging is basic motels rather than anything with a lobby. It is on the route because it sits at 495 feet on the Colorado, which makes it the warmest bed of the trip, and because it is genuinely on Route 66. If the party would rather have a proper room, Lake Havasu is 42 miles south — warmer weather is not the reason to go there, comfort is.
practical_notes.fuel: California fuel runs well above Nevada and Arizona. Fill up in Nevada before you drive in, top off in Barstow rather than inside Death Valley, where in-park fuel at Furnace Creek is notably expensive, and fill again in Arizona on the way home. The Amboy stretch of Route 66 has no fuel at all for about eighty miles.
practical_notes.death_valley_closures: Flood damage persists. Bonnie Clare Road and Scotty's Castle are closed with no reopening date, North Highway has loose gravel and missing shoulders, southern Badwater Road has soft shoulders and unpaved sections, and Emigrant Campground is closed indefinitely. Check the park's conditions page a week before departure.
practical_notes.fonts_point: The road to Font's Point is four miles of soft sand off the Borrego Salton Seaway. It needs four-wheel drive and it strands two-wheel-drive vehicles regularly. A minivan will not make it. Either rent something suitable for the day, take a local jeep tour, or accept that this one is off the list.
practical_notes.oatman_highway: The Oatman Highway over Sitgreaves Pass is steep with blind hairpins, and most rental agreements effectively prohibit it. It is passable but tight in a car and out of the question in a motorhome. The I-40 route through Kingman is the one in the plan, and it is ten miles longer but half an hour faster.
practical_notes.valley_of_fire: There is no hotel inside Valley of Fire. The park has two campgrounds — Atlatl Rock has hookups, Arch Rock does not — and both are reservation-only. In a car, the nearest rooms are in Overton about fifteen minutes away. This is the one stop where the motorhome build has the better night.
practical_notes.state_parks: The America the Beautiful pass covers Death Valley and Joshua Tree. It does not cover Anza-Borrego or the Salton Sea, which are California state parks, or Valley of Fire, which is a Nevada state park. None of them are expensive; they are just not free.

vehicle_restrictions.location: Death Valley — Artist's Drive and the final climb to Dante's View
vehicle_restrictions.impact_on_rv: A 30-footer is blocked. A C25 measures 24.93 ft — a three-inch margin, so measure the actual unit at pickup.

vehicle_restrictions.location: Route 66 — Oatman Highway over Sitgreaves Pass
vehicle_restrictions.rule: Steep with blind hairpins. Most rental agreements effectively prohibit it.
vehicle_restrictions.impact_on_rv: Avoid. Take I-40 through Kingman instead, which is the routing in the plan.
vehicle_restrictions.impact_on_car: Passable but tight, and worth doing for the burros. Check your rental agreement first.

vehicle_restrictions.rule: Most sites inside the park cap at around 25 to 35 feet and there are no hookups, no dump station and, at most campgrounds, no water.
vehicle_restrictions.impact_on_rv: Stay in Twentynine Palms instead, where a full-hookup site costs about the same and you can shower. The park's roads themselves are fine.

vehicle_restrictions.location: Anza-Borrego — the road to Font's Point
vehicle_restrictions.rule: Four miles of soft sand off the Borrego Salton Seaway. Four-wheel drive only.
vehicle_restrictions.impact_on_car: Blocked in a minivan or a two-wheel-drive SUV. This one is off the list for both builds unless you rent something else for the day.

money_savers.detail: Day use is $10 at the visitor centre and campground, and The Slot, Font's Point and every roadside trailhead are free. The Southwest Loop's equivalent — a guided slot canyon at Antelope — runs about $580 for six.
A hundred and thirty life-size metal sculptures — sloths, raptors, horses and a 350-foot serpent — scattered across open land around Borrego Springs. No gate, no ticket, no opening hours.

money_savers.item: Twentynine Palms instead of inside Joshua Tree
money_savers.detail: The park's own campgrounds have no hookups, no dump and mostly no water. A full-hookup site in town costs about the same as a dry site inside and you can shower — and you are ten minutes from the north entrance either way.
Buy bedding and kitchen gear at a Las Vegas store on day one for $200-300 and leave it behind. Cheaper than per-person kit fees for six.

money_savers.item: Go midweek in the Coachella Valley
money_savers.detail: January is peak season in Palm Springs and the weekend premium is steep. Arriving Sunday or Monday rather than Friday is the single biggest lever in the lodging line.

Covers Death Valley and Joshua Tree — both national parks on this route. It does NOT cover Anza-Borrego or the Salton Sea, which are California state parks, or Valley of Fire, which is a Nevada state park.

rejected_alternatives.reason: Santa Monica Pier is the western end of Route 66, and it slots between Barstow and Palm Springs for only 125 extra miles — genuinely cheap, and it would let the route run Route 66 from the Pacific to Arizona. Left out because the point of this trip is empty desert, and January is the wettest month of LA's year.

The better Route 66 town and the better rooms, but it sits at 3,366 feet and averages a January low of 0°C. It would be the one freezing night on a route built to avoid them. You drive through it and stop at the Powerhouse instead.

Warm, comfortable, and 42 miles off the Route 66 line. It is a lake town with a novelty bridge rather than anything to do with the road, and in January it is too cold to swim. It gets two nights on the Sonoran Loop instead.

rejected_alternatives.place: Zion, Bryce and the Grand Canyon
rejected_alternatives.reason: The famous parks on the Southwest Loop sit between 4,000 and 8,000 feet. Warm and high do not go together in January — that is the entire reason this route exists.
5,200 feet, freezing at night in January, and on the wrong side of the map. It belongs to the Southwest Loop.
Warmer still, and the giant saguaro grows nowhere on this route. But reaching Tucson from Las Vegas costs you a 288-mile day. That trip is the Sonoran Loop.
No hookups, no potable water, no cell service, and the York Fire burned close to 100,000 acres in 2023 including much of the Cima Dome Joshua tree forest.

Genuinely remarkable, and only twenty minutes past the south end of the Salton Sea — but routing the day through it costs 76 extra miles and two extra hours. It sits on the far shore from the road you are on.
Trailer rentals do not include a tow vehicle, and the major rental companies prohibit towing outright. Turo treats towing as a prohibited use that voids damage protection.

motorhome.name: Motorhome
motorhome.tagline: Cheapest, simplest, and no longer the cold one

vehicle.notes: Book by seatbelt count, not sleeping capacity. On this route there is no reason to take the smaller C25 for clearance — the only length limit you meet is Death Valley's 25 ft on Artist's Drive and Dante's View, and a C25 measures 24.93 ft, which is a three-inch margin you should not rely on.

pros: Food costs stay low because you cook
No freezing nights, so none of the winterising grief the Southwest Loop forces on you
Only two places on this route it cannot go, and both are in Death Valley
cons: Still barred from Artist's Drive and Dante's View, so it still needs a separate rental car in Death Valley
Cannot take the Oatman Highway over Sitgreaves Pass
Joshua Tree's own campgrounds are too small and have no hookups, so you sleep in town
Tanks fill fast with six people; plan a dump roughly every other night
Palm Springs and Borrego Springs RV parks are at their annual peak in January

car-and-lodging.name: Car and lodging
car-and-lodging.tagline: More expensive, more comfortable, and it unlocks the Oatman Highway

vehicle.notes: A minivan is better for people, a Suburban better for luggage. From Las Vegas, including airport concession fees. Neither will get you to Font's Point — that needs four-wheel drive.

pros: Unlocks the Oatman Highway and its burros
Real beds, and rooms you can spread six people across
Fuel drops to about a third of the motorhome's
No dump station, no propane, no levelling blocks
Artist's Drive and Dante's View without a second rental
cons: Separate lodging bookings to manage, in the region's most expensive month
Luggage for six in one vehicle is tight
